title: Adaptive Teaching: In Search of Conceptual Clarity
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans argues that 'adaptive teaching' has become so loosely defined in practice that it's indistinguishable from differentiation, inclusive teaching, or simply teaching well, and that this conceptual sprawl prevents it from being implemented with fidelity. He proposes a tight, precise definition: adaptive teaching is when a teacher actively and frequently seeks feedback on the impact of their teaching on all pupils during the lesson and adapts instruction accordingly to meet emerging needs -- deliberately narrower than the EEF's version, which also includes before-lesson planning. Evans situates this within a broader distinction between the 'universal offer' (inclusive-by-design teaching that should work for everyone, akin to dropped kerbs benefiting wheelchair users and everyone else) and 'different or extra' provision like differentiation, which he frames as a deficit model that should be minimized as the universal offer improves. He closes by cataloguing what adaptive teaching actually looks like in practice -- whole-class response strategies, cold calling, circulating and intervening -- and warns that broadening the term risks pulling teacher attention toward before-lesson individual accommodation rather than the harder, higher-impact skill of adapting live, in the moment.
points: Evans's precise definition -- adapting to moment-to-moment feedback during the lesson, not before-lesson planning -- deliberately excludes practices the EEF's broader definition includes, arguing the broader version pulls teacher attention toward the easier 'before' behaviors.

His dropped-kerb analogy reframes the universal offer: inclusive-by-design teaching should reduce the need for differentiation ('different or extra'), which he explicitly calls a deficit model that places the burden of adjustment on the pupil's difference rather than on instructional design.

The 'fish in the sea' framing -- adaptive teaching is one specific fish, inclusive teaching is the whole sea -- gives a memorable test for whether a practice belongs under 'adaptive teaching' or a neighboring term.

Evans explicitly separates adaptive teaching from modelling and scaffolding, arguing these get wrongly folded into descriptions of adaptive teaching when they more accurately belong under inclusive teaching.
quotes: I think we can all agree that naming things correctly is important. To do this, we must have a proper conception of what does and does not fall into a category.
Many teachers believe that adaptive teaching is differentiation re-named.
Better, I would argue, to say the teacher is adapting ‘to the feedback they receive moment to moment’.
If inclusive teaching is ‘things that swim in the sea’, adaptive teaching is ‘fish’.
DoE situates the deficit as a characteristic of the pupil, not the provision. It says to the pupil, ‘Because of the way you are, you need something different or extra to what most pupils need’.
Being precise and narrow in our focus prevents concept-creep and increases the likelihood that desirable practices will be adopted with fidelity.
